papers.title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data
papers.title_zh: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data
papers.tldr_zh: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of h
papers.cover_zh: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of h
papers.abstract_zh: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.

papers.title: A general-purpose safe manipulator planning framework for diverse environments without retraining
papers.title_zh: A general-purpose safe manipulator planning framework for diverse environments without retraining
papers.tldr_zh: Nowadays, robots need to be retrained whenever their operati
papers.cover_zh: Nowadays, robots need to be retrained whenever their operati
papers.abstract_zh: Nowadays, robots need to be retrained whenever their operating environment changes, and this prohibitive training cost keeps them far from daily use. The community is calling for innovations that bestow on a robot the ability to safely grasp different objects under different conditions without excessive training data and computing power. In response to this call, we present a general-purpose manipulator mission-planning framework, allowing a robot to safely perform manipulation tasks, such as grasping objects that fit in its gripper, across different operating environments without retraining its controllers. The framework rests on two innovations: a finite-state abstracted model, bisimilar to the original system dynamics, that describes accessibility of the space in front of the robot under its given arm and gripper, and a block-conservative specification generation method that turns each manipulation task under any specific operational environment into specifications about state accessibility of the abstracted model. A task proven feasible and safe on the abstracted model is guaranteed to be safe and achievable by the robot. Real-world case studies conducted on a Unitree G1 U1 humanoid show that manipulation tasks commonly encountered in daily life, such as grasping an object, pressing an elevator button or picking up a berry, can be handled within this framework, where an abstracted model of the G1 U1 robot is built only once to avoid costly model reconstructions, and different tasks are simply captured by specific block-conservative specifications, achievable by a generic mission planner with vision-based feedback control.

papers.title: FreshVLA: Frequency-Regularized Time Scale Hierarchical Latent Actions for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.title_zh: FreshVLA: Frequency-Regularized Time Scale Hierarchical Latent Actions for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr_zh: Learning reusable latent actions from action-free videos off
papers.cover_zh: Learning reusable latent actions from action-free videos off
papers.abstract_zh: Learning reusable latent actions from action-free videos offers an effective route to improving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. However, reconstruction-oriented latent actions do not necessarily benefit policy learning: as they may encode task-irrelevant static appearance with scene identity, or entangle slowly varying task progress with fine-grained execution dynamics in limited discrete code. We propose FreshVLA, a VLA framework built on a frequency-guided, dynamics-sensitive learning paradigm for acquiring temporally hierarchical continuous latent actions. FreshVLA uses a high-pass prior to guide visual transition encoding toward dynamical regions, thereby reducing reliance on static appearance cues. It further organizes latent actions into coarse-grained task progress and fine-grained execution dynamics through cross-timescale sampling and frequency-domain regularization, enhancing their capacity to represent long-horizon behaviors. During policy training, we freeze the pretrained latent action encoder and transfer its representations to robot control through joint flow-matching of latent and robot actions. FreshVLA achieves 98.2% average success on LIBERO and 98.0% on LIBERO-Long, exceeding GR00T-N1.6 on the latter by 3.6%. It also reaches an average sequence length of 4.52 on CALVIN and strong overall success rate of 80.4% in the zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluation. Furthermore, FreshVLA exhibits greater robustness to visual perturbations and a more distinct division of roles between two branches in modeling low- and high-frequency motion, respectively. In 35-step action regression, it achieves a 51.3-percentage-point higher relative error reduction than its hierarchical discrete counterpart. Real-world experiments demonstrate that FreshVLA improves the average success rate over $π_{0.5}$ by 7.5%. The FreshVLA project page is available at https://freshvla.github.io/.

papers.title: RoboJackVR: Turning Robot Tasks into VR Games for Scalable Demonstration Collection
papers.title_zh: RoboJackVR: Turning Robot Tasks into VR Games for Scalable Demonstration Collection
papers.tldr_zh: Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection sys
papers.cover_zh: Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection sys
papers.abstract_zh: Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection systems that accommodate more participants and diverse tasks, yet teleoperation barriers and task-adaptation effort limit this expansion. We present RoboJackVR, a standalone virtual reality (VR) game in which players manipulate simulated robots to execute combat skills and contribute demonstrations. MuJoCo simulation and demonstration recording run locally on the headset, removing the need for an external PC or simulation server during collection. Tutorials, skill selection, combat consequences, and character progression organize repeated task attempts within a continuing game. Task contracts declare assets, controls, resets, success criteria, and recording semantics; separate game configurations specify guidance, attempt groups, skill effects, and course placement. Shared bindings connect these declarations to task execution, outcome handling, and recording, allowing tasks to reuse the game flow while retaining their control and success semantics. Batch tools package supported resources and generate configurations, with manual adaptation and review for new interfaces and unsupported predicates. We instantiate the approach with SO101-Nexus-derived and LIBERO tasks. On the 66 LIBERO-90 tasks covered by the collected data, ACT policies trained solely on VR demonstrations retain approximately 91% of the full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline's success rate on held-out initial states, averaged over four training seeds. These results support the utility of play-collected VR demonstrations for policy learning in this setting.

papers.title: PROVE: Predict-to-Specify and Observe-to-Verify for Human-Aligned Evaluation of Mobile Manipulation
papers.title_zh: PROVE: Predict-to-Specify and Observe-to-Verify for Human-Aligned Evaluation of Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr_zh: Judging open-world robot manipulation is hard because layout
papers.cover_zh: Judging open-world robot manipulation is hard because layout
papers.abstract_zh: Judging open-world robot manipulation is hard because layouts, articulated fixtures, and valid goal configurations vary widely. On RoboCasa365, simulator predicates agree with human judgments on only 69.09\% of rollouts, and a frontier VLM judge on 86.12\%. We present textbf{PROVE} (Predict-to-Specify, Observe-to-Verify), which first specifies what success should look like and then checks the outcome. PROVE refines success conditions from the instruction, the initial scene, a target-object reference image, and a generated goal image. The goal image only sharpens the conditions and never serves as evidence. On 6,500 human-annotated rollouts over 65 atomic actions, PROVE reaches textbf{96.83\%} agreement. Applied to open-source policies, it reports far lower success than native checks and changes their ranking. To reduce evaluation overhead in policy learning, we distill PROVE into textbf{PROVE-Lite}, a 4B evaluator that needs no reference images. In one forward pass, PROVE-Lite predicts the outcome and the terminal state of each task condition. It reaches textbf{91.20\%} agreement while running about 38$×$ faster than PROVE. Mapped to a severity-aware reward, its diagnoses improve PPO post-training over both simulator and binary rewards.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
papers.title_zh: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
papers.tldr_zh: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adver
papers.cover_zh: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adver
papers.abstract_zh: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.

papers.title: Lab2Sim: Agentic Generation of Interactive Laboratory Equipment from Operation Videos
papers.title_zh: Lab2Sim: Agentic Generation of Interactive Laboratory Equipment from Operation Videos
papers.tldr_zh: Generating laboratory assets that faithfully reproduce the a
papers.cover_zh: Generating laboratory assets that faithfully reproduce the a
papers.abstract_zh: Generating laboratory assets that faithfully reproduce the appearance, structure, and joint motions of real equipment remains challenging. Existing asset generation methods struggle to directly generate simulation assets for all equipment observed in operation videos and to faithfully reproduce the appearance, joint motions, and internal cavities of the real equipment. To address the challenge, we present Lab2Sim, an agentic framework that generates editable, simulation-ready laboratory equipment assets from egocentric or multi-view operation videos. Lab2Sim comprises four specialized agents. The Evidence Agent combines video observations with laboratory knowledge to specify equipment parts, materials, and functional requirements, which guide the Asset Agent in constructing editable Blender assets. The independent Verifier checks the generated geometry and appearance against the evidence and requirements, providing targeted feedback for revision. The Simulation Integration Agent converts verified Blender assets into simulation instances with physical properties and articulated mechanisms, using execution feedback to refine their behavior. Experiments on human and robot laboratory scenes show that Lab2Sim achieves higher visual fidelity and stronger interaction capability than coding-agent and real-to-sim baselines, including a Codex baseline using the same underlying model. We further demonstrate valve-controlled drainage and use the generated asset library to reproduce laboratory scenes and operations in RoboTwin, supporting reusable simulation environments for robotic laboratory tasks.

papers.title: VivaWorld: Long-Horizon Video World Model With Compositional 3D Priors
papers.title_zh: VivaWorld: Long-Horizon Video World Model With Compositional 3D Priors
papers.tldr_zh: Long-horizon video generation is key to interactive world mo
papers.cover_zh: Long-horizon video generation is key to interactive world mo
papers.abstract_zh: Long-horizon video generation is key to interactive world modeling, physical intelligence, and spatial reasoning, yet maintaining geometric consistency and accurate camera control remains challenging without 3D grounding. We introduce textbf{VivaWorld}, a framework for generating geometry- and view-consistent long videos from an image. We first construct a compositional hybrid 3D representation that combines reconstructed point clouds, which preserve observed scene geometry and appearance, with generated textured meshes, which provide complete object geometry across $360^circ$ novel views. We also introduce a connected-region filter removing inconsistent floating components for robust cross-view reconstruction and propose a hybrid camera embedding that combines global and object-anchored Plücker rays to capture both scene-level camera motion and camera-object relationships, and inject it together with the visual guidance into a video generation model via a control adapter. Extensive experiments show VivaWorld achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and camera control, while supporting controllable novel-view synthesis, long-horizon scene exploration, and physical AI. Project page is available at: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/vivaworld/

papers.title: WorldUAV: Scaling UAV Data Synthesis via World Models
papers.title_zh: WorldUAV: Scaling UAV Data Synthesis via World Models
papers.tldr_zh: UAV detection and tracking remain constrained by the scarcit
papers.cover_zh: UAV detection and tracking remain constrained by the scarcit
papers.abstract_zh: UAV detection and tracking remain constrained by the scarcity of high-quality training data. Existing game-engine-based synthetic UAV data suffer from a substantial synthetic-to-real gap, while the high cost of manually collected real-world UAV data limits dataset scale. Therefore, we introduce WorldUAV, a high-quality UAV dataset constructed through an efficient framework powered by world models. Specifically, WorldUAV directly integrates UAVs into readily available real-world videos, naturally preserving realistic backgrounds, illumination, and scene dynamics. Leveraging the spatiotemporal priors of world models, it generates UAV videos with plausible motion, pose variations, and cross-frame consistency, effectively narrowing the gap between synthetic and real data. We further develop an agentic pipeline orchestrated by a multimodal large language model that acquires sources, plans UAV trajectories, invokes synthesis, and verifies generated videos, enabling fully automated dataset construction. WorldUAV comprises 6,878 UAV videos and 205,778 UAV images. Experiments show that WorldUAV significantly improves the performance of UAV detectors. Moreover, it substantially reduces dataset construction costs, requiring only 15 seconds and USD 0.0005 API cost per high-quality UAV image. Our work offers both a high-quality dataset and a scalable data generation paradigm for UAV detection and tracking.

papers.title: GeoTex: Geometry-as-Texture Encoding and History-Grounded 4D Occupancy Forecasting
papers.title_zh: GeoTex: Geometry-as-Texture Encoding and History-Grounded 4D Occupancy Forecasting
papers.tldr_zh: 4D occupancy forecasting models 3D scene evolution to suppor
papers.cover_zh: 4D occupancy forecasting models 3D scene evolution to suppor
papers.abstract_zh: 4D occupancy forecasting models 3D scene evolution to support future prediction and scenario generation in autonomous-driving world models. Semantic occupancy abstracts image color and texture into discrete labels, leaving 3D voxel arrangements as the primary cues for distinguishing local shapes within each class. Existing methods borrow image-encoding frameworks to obtain compact latent representations through height channelization or plane factorization, but do not sufficiently model within-column height patterns and cross-column relations jointly before compression, weakening these geometric cues. Forecasting also underutilizes complementary history and struggles to retain reliable observation evidence. We therefore propose GeoTex, an occupancy world model combining geometry-as-texture encoding with history-grounded forecasting. GeoTex Representation jointly encodes within-column height patterns and cross-column relations into compact continuous latent representations and restores 3D structure through content-dependent height unfolding and geometric interaction. GeoTex Prediction retains initial evidence throughout rollout in fixed cross-observation relational memory and incorporates complementary recent history through target-referenced residual updates. After prediction training, decoder-only adaptation improves semantic decoding of predicted states. GeoTex improves average forecasting mIoU and IoU by 9.79% and 11.91% relative to GenieDrive while reducing parameters from 3.47M to 2.33M, with gains increasing at longer horizons. Code is included in the supplementary material.

papers.title: DualCast: Dual-Image Conditioned Diffusion Transformers for Digital Human E-Commerce Video Generation
papers.title_zh: DualCast: Dual-Image Conditioned Diffusion Transformers for Digital Human E-Commerce Video Generation
papers.tldr_zh: Recent advances in world models for game interaction and con
papers.cover_zh: Recent advances in world models for game interaction and con
papers.abstract_zh: Recent advances in world models for game interaction and control have increased the demand for large-scale gameplay videos paired with camera trajectories. However, capturing synchronized camera trajectories often requires game-specific pipelines, limiting scalability. We therefore propose GameWeaver, a unified diffusion framework that automatically produces paired video--camera data through three complementary tasks: camera pose estimation from observed video, video generation along a prescribed camera trajectory, and joint video--camera generation from a reference image and text. First, each tipxel stores the normalized 3D coordinates of a pixel ray's endpoint in a reference coordinate frame. The resulting three-channel tipxel fields and RGB frames share the pretrained video model's VAE. Next, a fully trainable dual-stream Transformer exchanges appearance and geometry features through bidirectional gated attention and conditions both streams on shared text features. Finally, deterministic fitting recovers camera intrinsics and normalized trajectories from generated tipxel fields. In our evaluation tasks, GameWeaver achieves a normalized translation MSE of 0.0029 for camera control; for joint generation, it scores 85.48 out of 100 on instruction adherence versus 64.71 for the best cascade on that metric, validating the feasibility of the proposed approach.

papers.title: RegHarness: Regulating What Code-as-Policy Agents Keep from Steps to Skills
papers.title_zh: RegHarness: Regulating What Code-as-Policy Agents Keep from Steps to Skills
papers.tldr_zh: Code-as-Policy agents generate, execute, and revise robot pr
papers.cover_zh: Code-as-Policy agents generate, execute, and revise robot pr
papers.abstract_zh: Code-as-Policy agents generate, execute, and revise robot programs, but often lack explicit mechanisms to govern what persists across executions: which actions are retained within a trial and which code modifications carry over to subsequent runs. This leaves two critical aspects of agent behavior insufficiently controlled: step-level execution and cross-run adaptation. We present RegHarness, a two-level harness that governs both forms of persistence for the RATs agent team, without relying on a vision-language-action (VLA) policy or demonstrations. Within each trial, run-time governance evaluates each proposed step from a reset scene, replaying the committed steps, while a fixed-rule controller commits the step only when both RATs' verifier and a task-long LLM auditor approve it. Between runs, a coding agent uses logged failures to develop and test revisions to skills, primitives, and rules, which remain disabled by default until explicitly enabled by the authors. Using a single low-cost model across all run-time roles, RegHarness achieves an 87.8% success rate (158/180) on paired LIBERO-PRO trials, compared with 39.4% for RATs, and a 72.0% success rate on MolmoSpaces trials. A $2×2$ ablation study of RegHarness's two levels shows that its skill refinement alone increases RATs' successful trials from 71 to 135, whereas run-time governance alone achieves 105 and RATs' native stepwise reset-and-replay mode achieves only 46. These findings suggest that, for Code-as-Policy agents operating with low-cost models, task success depends not only on how generated programs are executed, but also on the quality of the reusable skills they invoke and how those skills evolve across runs.

papers.title: WhatIf: Counterfactual World Models over Action-Grounded Causal Graphs for Robotic Manipulation
papers.title_zh: WhatIf: Counterfactual World Models over Action-Grounded Causal Graphs for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr_zh: World models predict what happens under an action, but choos
papers.cover_zh: World models predict what happens under an action, but choos
papers.abstract_zh: World models predict what happens under an action, but choosing between actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation. Factual transitions alone determine action-wise marginal futures and average effects, but not individual effects or the probability that switching actions causes harm. We introduce WhatIf, a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from factual history. Each candidate action induces a sparse object-factor causal graph describing the physical pathways it activates. Rolling out these graphs under the shared situation anchors predictions to observed outcomes and confines action contrasts to the objects each action reaches. Shared type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects, while a round-trip loss enforces action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels. We show that replacing an individual effect with its conditional mean incurs mean-squared error equal to its conditional variance, motivating comparisons between coupled futures. Building on these comparisons, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations and constrains the probability of harm. Paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of $1-ρ$, where $ρ$ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and cancel model errors shared by both branches. Each executed transition provides hindsight advantages to update the physics posterior, the next plan, and an amortized policy without a learned critic. We further establish when observational transitions identify interventional dynamics. Paired simulator interventions evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, and decision quality.

papers.title: Skeptic: Grounding Failure Diagnosis for Robot Skill Discovery
papers.title_zh: Skeptic: Grounding Failure Diagnosis for Robot Skill Discovery
papers.tldr_zh: Robot agents discover reusable skills by revising programs f
papers.cover_zh: Robot agents discover reusable skills by revising programs f
papers.abstract_zh: Robot agents discover reusable skills by revising programs from execution feedback and retaining experience for later tasks. This process can fail when an agent treats an unsuccessful program as evidence that the task is physically impossible, ending exploration with revision budget remaining. We study this failure in Qwen3.8-27B and examine two decisions that shape skill discovery: I) how execution failures are diagnosed, and II) which lessons enter the shared skill library. Failure diagnosis requires the agent to reconstruct physical action effects from multimodal traces, while independent reproduction of a proposed repair does not require adequate task performance from its source program. We introduce Skeptic, a training-free protocol that uses measured action outcomes to guide repair and measured task success to govern skill admission. A grounded event log reports action effects and object end states from depth images and proprioception, separating sensor observations from inferred diagnoses. Verified promotion adds a development-success requirement on the source program to the existing independent reproduction check. Across 60 audited tasks, the mean number of tasks with false impossibility judgments decreases from 19.5 to 8.5 per campaign. On 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and seven Robosuite tasks, Skeptic improves held-out success by 14.9 and 11.7 percentage points, with frozen model weights and the same program-revision budget.

papers.title: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
papers.title_zh: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
papers.tldr_zh: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that
papers.cover_zh: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that
papers.abstract_zh: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically naïve animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.

papers.title: $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM: Efficient Hierarchical Memory Across Modalities and Timescales for World-Action Models
papers.title_zh: $mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM: Efficient Hierarchical Memory Across Modalities and Timescales for World-Action Models
papers.tldr_zh: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires historical contex
papers.cover_zh: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires historical contex
papers.abstract_zh: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires historical context, yet retaining extensive visual histories incurs growing storage and retrieval costs, while aggressive compression risks losing fine-grained information needed for subsequent decisions. Moreover, executed action histories capture intermediate behaviors that sparse visual observations may miss. Preserving this complementary context efficiently calls for modality-specific memory mechanisms that balance recent detail with long-term retention. To this end, we introduce $mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM, a world-action model equipped with hierarchical visual and interaction memories. $mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM preserves recent visual observations in dense short-term memory while consolidating entries evicted from this window into fixed-size associative long-term memory through gated delta updates. Within the same short- and long-term hierarchy, interaction memory encodes executed action prefixes into compact temporal representations, complementing visual observations with behavioral context. These complementary memories are integrated into world-action modeling through layer-wise retrieval, enabling memory-augmented action generation with a bounded online memory footprint independent of episode length. On the memory-dependent simulation benchmarks MIKASA-Robo and RMBench, $mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves +53.2% and +61.2% absolute improvements in average success rates over Fast-WAM, respectively. These gains extend to real-world manipulation, where $mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves a +29.3% absolute improvement over LingBot-VA in average success across three tasks. These results suggest that $mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM offers a promising approach to efficient memory-augmented world-action modeling.

papers.title: Practice Makes Fluent: Learning to Use Earlier Predictions in Looped Models
papers.title_zh: Practice Makes Fluent: Learning to Use Earlier Predictions in Looped Models
papers.tldr_zh: People become faster at a task through practice, but models
papers.cover_zh: People become faster at a task through practice, but models
papers.abstract_zh: People become faster at a task through practice, but models that improve with experience do not necessarily learn to use less computation. We train looped models, whose intermediate predictions allow earlier exits, to perform tasks with fewer iterations through practice. This is difficult because shared-weight updates can degrade the final-loop prediction while improving early ones, and the exit gate must track early predictions as their quality changes. We propose FLUENT, which requires no additional task labels or rewards: it distills the initial model's final-loop prediction into early predictions, anchors the current final-loop prediction to the same frozen teacher, and trains the exit gate to balance disagreement with the current final-loop prediction against computation cost. FLUENT improves performance at shallower depth in new Crafter worlds, raises LIBERO success with fewer action-head iterations, and maintains language-model accuracy at lower selected depth. On a real robot, success rises from 62.3\% to 74.6\% while mean time over successful episodes falls from 69\,s to 31\,s. The project page is available at https://msseok96-cpu.github.io/FLUENT/.
